title: India's Bonds Just Had Their Best Month in Seven Years. The World's Biggest Index May Be Next.
excerpt: After scrapping all taxes on foreign bond investment, India attracted a record $3.16 billion in June. Now Bloomberg index inclusion is on the horizon — and the real flood hasn't started yet.
body:
Foreign investors poured a record $3.16 billion into Indian government bonds in June — more in a single month than in the entire first five months of 2026 combined. The buying spree, triggered by India's decision to scrap all taxes on foreign bond investment, has pushed the benchmark 10-year yield to its steepest monthly decline in nearly seven years and put India on the cusp of joining one of the world's most important bond indexes.

The speed of the reversal has surprised even seasoned fund managers. As recently as April, India was bleeding capital. Foreign portfolio investors had pulled $28 billion from Indian equities since the start of the year, the rupee had hit a record low, and Brent crude — spiking above $120 a barrel during the Iran war — was squeezing India's import bill and current account.

The Tax Move That Changed Everything

On June 5, the Reserve Bank of India and the Finance Ministry unveiled a coordinated package designed to stanch the outflow. The centrepiece: scrapping the 12.5% long-term capital gains tax and the 20% withholding tax on interest income for foreign investors in government bonds.

The move was unprecedented. India had been one of the few major economies that still taxed non-resident bond investments, putting it at a structural disadvantage against peers like Indonesia, South Korea, and Mexico that offer tax-free access.

"These changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets. "Removing the tax element will ease some of the operational frictions for investors."

The numbers bear that out. In the three sessions after the announcement, more than $1 billion flowed in. By month's end, the tally had tripled. The Fully Accessible Route — the category of Indian bonds open to unlimited foreign investment — absorbed ₹29,900 crore ($3.16 billion), a record since the RBI created it.

> ""These changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets."

Bloomberg Index: The Prize on the Horizon

The real payoff may still be ahead. Indian FAR bonds are already included in three major emerging-market debt indexes, including J.P. Morgan's GBI-EM Global Diversified, which triggered phased inflows of billions when India was added in June 2024.

But the big prize is the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, the world's most widely tracked fixed-income benchmark with an estimated $70 trillion in assets benchmarked to it. Bloomberg had deferred India's inclusion earlier this year, citing the tax burden and operational frictions. Those objections have now largely been addressed.

![Finance Ministry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cd/Government-Vedder-Highsmith-detail-1.jpeg)

"The recent measures address some of the roadblocks to inclusion, particularly the tax issue, as India has now aligned itself with other zero-tax sovereign issuers included in this index," said Shiv Chopra, senior portfolio manager at BNP Paribas Asset Management. "Liquidity and market depth have also now been improved."

Traders are now watching for Bloomberg Index Services' decision, which could come as early as this quarter. Analysts estimate that inclusion could eventually bring $10 billion to $20 billion in passive inflows, dwarfing June's record.

Oil's Tailwind

The bond rally has been turbocharged by a collapse in oil prices. Brent crude has fallen more than 21% in June alone, retreating to about $72 a barrel — back to pre-Iran-war levels and well below the late-April peak of $126.

For India, which imports nearly 90% of its crude, the oil slide is a direct fiscal and balance-of-payments relief. HSBC now forecasts a $25 billion balance-of-payments surplus for the current financial year ending March 2027, after two consecutive years of deficit.

"The all-in FX package to attract inflows and the fall in oil prices have flipped the BoP outlook," the bank wrote in a note.

What This Means for NRIs and Diaspora Investors

The tax reforms don't just benefit institutional investors. The RBI's June 5 package also includes incentives for banks to raise foreign currency deposits from Non-Resident Indians — a critical funding source during previous episodes of rupee stress. NRI deposits stood at about $145 billion before the announcement.

For diaspora investors considering Indian fixed-income assets, the removal of capital gains and withholding taxes makes government bonds significantly more attractive on a relative basis. The 10-year benchmark yield, currently around 6.74%, offers a substantial premium over U.S. Treasuries, and the rupee's stabilisation has reduced currency risk.

The question now is whether the momentum can hold. If Bloomberg grants inclusion and oil prices remain subdued, India's bond market could see its most transformative year since liberalisation. If not, the record June may prove to be a one-off sprint rather than the start of a marathon.

*Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Asset Management*
